rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention window will guide subsequent window trimming and slope or temperature tests.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be retained with faster elution, keeping the maximum-scoring method as the fallback.
Shorten the gradient another grid step while holding selectivity variables fixed. The minimum resolution of 3.24 leaves substantial margin to preserve the maximum CRF with a shorter run.

Test the next shorter gradient with the solvent window and temperature unchanged. The observed resolution trend suggests the closest pair may remain above 1.5, preserving maximum CRF while shortening elution further.

The 4-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for further steepening. Test higher temperature at the same slope to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves or worsens the critical pair.

Return to the temperature that preserved full resolution and trim the low-organic portion of the gradient. Raising phi0 while keeping it below the estimated first-peak elution fraction of 0.27 tests faster elution with a shallower gradient slope.

Test the shortest permitted gradient at lower temperature, which may offset compression of the critical early pair because heating reduced its resolution. Previously validated methods already secure the maximum CRF; this tests whether it is attainable with substantially faster elution.

Narrow the gradient window by raising phi0, reducing the slope while retaining the strong final solvent for the last peak. This tests whether the critical pair can gain the small amount of resolution needed for maximum CRF at a 2-minute gradient.

Injection 8 achieves maximum CRF with the shortest allowed gradient. Raise temperature one grid step to test a further retention-time reduction while checking whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

Raise phi0 one grid step to test whether the narrower gradient restores the critical pair's small resolution deficit while shortening late retention. Monitor the early peaks for loss of retention; injection 8 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.
Test one temperature step above the fastest validated maximum-CRF method to locate its resolution boundary. Keep phi0 fixed because the first peak is already close to the unretained region.

Reduce gradient steepness at 35 C to recover resolution of the early pair without raising phi0 further. The last peak may move into the final hold, but the modest endpoint reduction should keep it well within the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The critical early pair barely improved with a shallower gradient at 35 C, so test lower temperature to recover selectivity instead. This should provide greater resolution margin than injection 10 while retaining a short elution time and the maximum CRF.

Lower phi0 to retain the early pair more strongly and modestly reduce phi1 to compensate with a shallower slope. Relative to injection 9, this tests whether a single endpoint step restores full resolution while maintaining rapid elution.

Combine the favorable low-temperature selectivity with a shallower 2-minute gradient to increase resolution margin while keeping the first peak retained. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF alternative to the fastest validated method, injection 10.

Test the upper starting-organic boundary at the temperature with the best early-pair selectivity. This may shorten elution further, but the first peak could become insufficiently retained; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF fallback.

Lower phi0 to keep the early peaks comfortably retained while preserving the shortest gradient and strong endpoint. Results at phi0 0.15 and 0.25 bracket this setting, suggesting it may achieve maximum CRF with elution near 2.7 minutes.

Test the intermediate endpoint between injections 8 and 15 to balance rapid elution with additional critical-pair resolution margin. Both bracketing methods achieved maximum CRF, making this a promising refinement without approaching the early-peak retention boundary.

Refine around injection 10, the fastest validated maximum-CRF method, by reducing phi1 one grid step. This tests whether modestly gentler elution adds critical-pair resolution margin at only a small time cost.

Raise temperature one step from injection 15 to shorten its final hold while testing whether its resolution margin remains sufficient. This explores another maximum-CRF method with better early retention than injection 10, which remains the fastest validated option.

Reduce phi1 one step from injection 17 to improve its marginal early-pair resolution while keeping both early peaks well retained. This should preserve maximum CRF with a short run and provide an alternative less sensitive to excessive starting organic.

Combine the favorable selectivity of injection 13 with a slightly shallower gradient to test added resolution margin at a modest time cost. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 10 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Test one lower endpoint from injection 22 to increase critical-pair resolution margin while retaining the shortest programmed gradient. The neighboring results suggest full resolution and elution near 3 minutes; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Raise temperature one grid step from injection 23 to shorten late elution while using its resolution margin. The adjacent temperature results suggest this untested setting can retain maximum CRF; injection 10 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Use the final injection to test a nearby method expected to preserve maximum CRF, with stronger early retention and a shallower slope than injection 21. The campaign has already reached the score ceiling; injection 10 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method at t_last 2.58 minutes.
